pos: n. (the electorate of Wittenberg, where the Reformation began, and whose division between two Saxon houses nearly destroyed it)
etymology: Latin Saxonia, from the Saxons; German Sachsen. The lands were divided in 1485 between the Ernestine and Albertine lines of the house of Wettin.
biblical_def: Saxony is where the Reformation began and where it was first betrayed from inside. Wittenberg, in Ernestine or electoral Saxony, held the university at which Luther taught from 1512 and the church door on which the ninety-five theses were posted in 1517; Frederick the Wise protected him, John the Steadfast presented the Augsburg Confession in 1530, and John Frederick led the Schmalkaldic League. Ducal or Albertine Saxony, under Duke George, stayed Catholic until 1539. Then in 1546 Duke Maurice of Albertine Saxony took the emperor's side against his own cousin and co-religionist for the promise of the electoral title; the League was broken at Muhlberg in 1547, John Frederick was imprisoned, and Maurice received the electorate. It was Maurice's Saxony that then accepted the Leipzig Interim of 1548, conceding the restoration of Catholic ceremonies, bishops and much of the mass on the ground that these were things indifferent, adiaphora, which a church might yield to keep the peace. Matthias Flacius and the strict Lutherans refused, the quarrel split the Lutheran churches for thirty years, and the Formula of Concord settled it in 1577 against the Interim. The dictionary enters Saxony because the Reformation's birthplace produced its sharpest lesson: that a concession called indifferent is not indifferent when it is demanded as the price of surrender.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an interim as the meantime or intervening time; adiaphora as things indifferent; an elector as a prince entitled to vote for the emperor; and a concession as the act of yielding.
webster_full: INTERIM, n. The meantime; the intervening time; a temporary arrangement made until a final settlement.
INDIFFERENT, a. Neither good nor bad; having no influence or preponderating weight; of a middle nature.
ELECTOR, n. A prince of the German empire who had a voice in the election of the emperor.
CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding; the thing yielded, usually implying a demand or claim.
CEREMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion; the forms of civility; outward form.
scriptures: Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Col 2:16
Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Electorate of Wittenberg where the Reformation began, divided between Ernestine and Albertine houses, whose Leipzig Interim of 1548 conceded ceremonies as things indifferent.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the yielding of a thing truly indifferent at the moment when yielding it is a confession of defeat. The Leipzig Interim's defenders were not wrong that vestments and feast days are not commanded or forbidden in themselves; they were wrong that a ceremony demanded by a victorious enemy as the sign of submission is still merely a ceremony. The apostle makes the distinction himself: he circumcised Timothy freely and refused Titus absolutely, and of the latter case he says “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour” (Gal 2:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that liberty is to be stood in and not traded. “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1) is the command Flacius acted on, and the dictionary judges that he was right and Melanchthon's party wrong, while recording that their motive was the preservation of the churches and not cowardice. The rule for things genuinely indifferent remains, that no man is to judge another “in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday” (Col 2:16), and the rule for the rest is to “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).

pos: n. (the north German electorate of the Hohenzollerns, Lutheran from 1539 and Reformed in its elector from 1613, which took in the Huguenots in 1685)
etymology: German Brandenburg, from the Slavic fortress of Brennaburg on the Havel; the march was a frontier against the Wends.
biblical_def: Brandenburg is the electorate in which a Reformed prince had to govern a Lutheran people, and the arrangement that resulted taught Germany something about toleration. The march became Lutheran under Joachim II in 1539, with a church order that kept much of the old ceremonial. In 1613 the elector John Sigismund went over to the Reformed confession; his subjects and their clergy did not, and his attempt to impose it in 1614 produced riots in Berlin. He abandoned the attempt, and from then the Hohenzollerns ruled as Reformed princes over a Lutheran establishment, which forced them into a practical toleration of two Protestant confessions that no other German state had to work out. The fruit of that habit came in 1685. Six days after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, Frederick William, the Great Elector, issued the Edict of Potsdam inviting the French Reformed into his lands with ten years free of taxes, assistance in building houses, their own churches and ministers, and the right to use their own language; some twenty thousand Huguenots came, with their trades, and a sixth of Berlin was French-speaking within a generation. The dictionary enters Brandenburg because a prince who could not impose his confession learned to shelter other men's, and the Huguenots were the beneficiaries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an edict as a public ordinance of a sovereign; to revoke as to repeal or annul; an asylum as a place of refuge; and an immunity as freedom from an obligation.
webster_full: EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order; a decree.
REVOKE, v. To retract; to repeal; to reverse; to annul by a subsequent decision or act.
ASYLUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors found shelter; any place of retreat and security.
IMMUNITY, n. Freedom or exemption from obligation; particular privilege or prerogative.
MARCH, n. A border; a frontier; the confine or limit of a territory.

Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
corruption_summary: North German electorate, Lutheran from 1539 and Reformed in its elector from 1613, whose Edict of Potsdam in 1685 took in some twenty thousand Huguenots.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the forcing of a confession on a people by a prince, which John Sigismund attempted in 1614 and which the dictionary holds to be wrong even when the confession forced is the better one. Brandenburg was Lutheran and its elector became Reformed; the riots in Berlin were the people's answer to being reformed by decree. He gave it up, and the grudging coexistence that followed is what afterwards made room for the French. The law given to Israel about the sojourner is the standard Brandenburg eventually met: “the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you” (Lev 19:34).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of welcome, and the reason given for it in the law is memory of one's own exile: “Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deu 10:19). The Edict of Potsdam of 1685 was issued by a prince who knew what it was to be a minority in his own capital. Of such a reception the Lord says “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35), and the apostolic charge is to “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2).

pos: n. (the Baltic duchy whose son Johannes Bugenhagen wrote the church orders of northern Germany and Scandinavia)
etymology: Latin Pomerania, from the Slavic po more, along the sea; German Pommern, the coast between the Oder and the Vistula.
biblical_def: Pomerania is the Baltic duchy that gave the Reformation its chief organiser of churches. Johannes Bugenhagen, born at Wollin in 1485, was a Pomeranian schoolmaster and priest who read Luther's book on the captivity of the church in 1520, went to Wittenberg, became pastor of the town church there and Luther's own confessor, and then spent twenty years writing church ordinances: for Brunswick in 1528, Hamburg in 1529, Lubeck in 1531, Pomerania itself in 1535, Denmark in 1537, Schleswig-Holstein in 1542, Hildesheim in 1544. The pattern was always the same and always practical: a superintendent over the ministers, preaching and catechising in the vernacular, a common chest out of the old church revenues for the poor and for scholarships, and a Latin school and a girls' school in every town. Pomerania's own dukes adopted the Reformation at the diet of Treptow in 1534 and Bugenhagen's ordinance the year after; the university of Greifswald was restored on it. He also married early and publicly, crowned Christian III of Denmark, and preached at Luther's funeral. The dictionary enters Pomerania because the Reformation needed a man who would write down the arrangements, and the man it got was a schoolmaster from the Baltic coast.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as a rule established by authority; a chest as a box for keeping valuables or money; a superintendent as one having oversight; and a scholarship as a maintenance for a scholar.
webster_full: ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
CHEST, n. A box of wood or other material, in which goods are kept or transported; a coffer for money.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
SCHOLARSHIP, n. The maintenance or stipend of a scholar; literature; learning; erudition.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food or clothing.
scriptures: Act 6:1
And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
Gal 2:10
Only they would that we should remember the poor; the same which I also was forward to do.
corruption_summary: Baltic duchy, reformed at the diet of Treptow in 1534, whose son Johannes Bugenhagen wrote the church orders of northern Germany and Scandinavia.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is a reformation that closes the monasteries and forgets the poor they fed. Bugenhagen's ordinances all answer it the same way, by taking the confiscated revenues into a common chest administered by the town for the relief of the poor, the support of ministers and the schooling of children, which is the first systematic Protestant poor law in Europe. The precedent is in Acts, where the complaint of the neglected widows was met by appointing men to the business, since there arose “a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected” (Act 6:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that care for the destitute is part of religion and not an appendix to it. “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) is the definition, and the apostolic agreement at Jerusalem included the charge “that we should remember the poor” (Gal 2:10). The duty begins at home, since a man who provides not for his own “hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8), and Bugenhagen's common chest was built to catch those his own could not.

pos: n. (the Baltic land of the Teutonic Order, secularised by Albert in 1525 as the first Lutheran state in Europe)
etymology: Latin Prussia, from the Prussians or Borussi, the Baltic people conquered by the Teutonic Order; German Preussen.
biblical_def: Prussia is where a crusading military order turned itself into a Lutheran duchy, the first state in Europe to be formally Protestant. The Teutonic Order had ruled the land since the thirteenth century; its last grand master in Prussia, Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach, met Luther at Wittenberg in 1523, was advised by him to lay down the habit, marry and govern as a secular prince, and did exactly that, taking the duchy as a Polish fief in 1525 and establishing the Reformation at once. Johann Briesmann and Paul Speratus organised the churches, Konigsberg's university was founded in 1544, and the duchy became the printing and training centre for the whole eastern Baltic: Polish books by Jan Seklucjan and Jan Malecki, and the first books ever printed in Lithuanian and in Old Prussian, were produced there for the duchy's own non-German subjects. Albert also sheltered men whose doctrine was not sound, and the Osiandrian controversy over whether justification is by Christ's indwelling divine righteousness rather than his imputed obedience was fought out at Konigsberg in the 1550s, the duke backing Osiander against his own faculty. The dictionary enters Prussia because the first Lutheran state showed both what a converted ruler could do and what a ruler who thinks himself a theologian will do.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to secularise as to convert from sacred to common use; a fief as an estate held of a superior; imputation as the reckoning of something to a person; and a grand master as the chief of a military order.
webster_full: SECULARIZE, v. To convert from spiritual or ecclesiastical appropriation to secular or common use.
FIEF, n. A fee; an estate held of a superior on condition of military service; a feud.
IMPUTATION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; the reckoning of anything to a person.
GRAND MASTER, n. The chief of a military order, as of the Knights Templars or the Teutonic Knights.
HABIT, n. Garment; dress; the dress or garb of a religious order.
scriptures: Rom 4:5
But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
Phi 3:9
And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:
Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
corruption_summary: Baltic land of the Teutonic Order, secularised by Albert in 1525 as Europe's first Lutheran state, and the seat of the Osiandrian controversy over justification.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is Osiandrianism, which located a sinner's justifying righteousness in the divine nature of the indwelling Christ rather than in his obedience reckoned to the believer, and so made justification a quality formed in the man instead of a verdict pronounced over him. Scripture puts the righteousness outside and the reckoning inside: God “justifieth the ungodly” (Rom 4:5) while he is still ungodly, and Christ was made sin for us “that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). Duke Albert backed Osiander against his own theologians, which is what a prince who takes sides in doctrine usually achieves.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the imputation of an obedience not our own, which is what the apostle means by a righteousness he disclaims owning: “not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ” (Phi 3:9). The ground of it is the second Adam's obedience, that “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). Prussia's better record is the printing: the first books in Lithuanian and Old Prussian came off its presses for peasants nobody else was going to teach.

pos: n. (the northern Baltic province whose German masters took the Reformation in 1524 and whose Estonian Bible came only in 1739)
etymology: Latin Estonia, from the Aestii named by Tacitus; Estonian Eesti, a Finnic tongue unrelated to the German of its rulers.
biblical_def: Estonia is the Baltic province where the Reformation arrived quickly for the rulers and slowly for the people. Reval and Dorpat, German Hanseatic towns under the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order, had evangelical preaching by 1523 and 1524, iconoclastic riots followed, and the town councils carried the Reformation through within a few years; a Lutheran establishment was in place while the Estonian-speaking peasantry remained serfs of German landlords who had no particular interest in teaching them. The gap between the two was closed slowly and by individual labour. Heinrich Stahl published an Estonian handbook and sermon collection from 1632, Anton thor Helle produced the first complete Estonian Bible in 1739, and the decisive change came through the Moravians, whose Estonian-speaking lay preachers from the 1730s reached the peasantry as the established church had not in two centuries. Balthasar Russow, himself of Estonian descent, wrote the chronicle of Livonia in German and recorded the peasants' condition with a candour his class did not share. The dictionary enters Estonia because it shows a Reformation complete in law and two hundred years late in the language of the people, and because the lesson is that a confession in a ruler's tongue converts the ruler.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a serf as a servile tenant attached to the soil; a chronicle as a historical account of facts in order of time; a vassal as one who holds land of a superior; and a handbook as a manual.
webster_full: SERF, n. A servant or slave employed in husbandry, and in some countries attached to the soil, and transferred with it.
CHRONICLE, n. An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
VASSAL, n. A feudatory; a tenant; one who holds land of a superior and vows fidelity and homage to him.
MANUAL, n. A small book, such as may be carried in the hand or conveniently handled.
PEASANTRY, n. Peasants; rustics; the body of countrymen, or tillers of the earth.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Jam 2:1
My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
corruption_summary: Northern Baltic province whose German towns reformed by 1524 while the Estonian peasantry waited until 1739 for a complete Bible in their own tongue.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the respect of persons that lets a church be thorough for its gentry and negligent for its serfs. Estonia's Lutheran establishment was settled, catechised and preached to in German within a decade; the people who worked the land got an Estonian Bible two hundred and fifteen years later. The apostle's prohibition is exact and was ignored: “have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (Jam 2:1). A ministry that will not learn the language of the poor has made that choice whatever it professes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching must reach the hearer in his own speech, or it is not preaching to him. “how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9) is the question Estonian peasants could have asked of a German sermon for two centuries, and the Pentecostal gift was given to answer it, that men hear “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8). The chain of necessity runs back to the sender, for “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14), and the Moravian lay preachers of the 1730s were the first to go.

pos: n. (the commonwealth whose Warsaw Confederation of 1573 granted the widest religious liberty in Europe, and which lost the Reformation anyway)
etymology: Latin Polonia, from the Polanie, the field-dwellers, from Slavic pole, a field; Polish Polska.
biblical_def: Poland is the kingdom in which the Reformation had every advantage and squandered them. By the 1560s a majority of the senate and a great part of the nobility were Protestant; Lutheranism held the German towns of the north, the Reformed held Lesser Poland and Lithuania under patrons like the Radziwills, the Bohemian Brethren held Great Poland, and John a Lasco returned from England in 1556 to try to unite them. The Consensus of Sandomierz in 1570 brought Lutheran, Reformed and Brethren into a mutual recognition, and the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, sworn by the nobility at the election of a new king, guaranteed that no one would be harmed for his religion, the broadest such guarantee in sixteenth-century Europe. It still failed. The Reformed never built a national confession, a single church order, or a university; the Polish Brethren split away into open antitrinitarianism and were expelled in 1658; and the Jesuits, given the schools, educated the sons of Protestant nobles back into the Roman church within two generations. The dictionary enters Poland because liberty and a sympathetic aristocracy were not enough, and what was missing was the unglamorous apparatus: a confession, a synod that could discipline, and schools of its own.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confederation as a league or alliance; a consensus as agreement; a senate as an assembly of counsellors; and discipline as instruction and government.
webster_full: CONFEDERATION, n. The act of confederating; a league; a compact for mutual support; alliance.
CONSENT, n. Agreement of minds; accord; concurrence in opinion or sentiment.
SENATE, n. An assembly or council of citizens invested with a share in the government of a state.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to rules; the system by which a church orders its members.
NOBILITY, n. The quality of being noble; the persons collectively who possess titles of nobility.
scriptures: And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Let all things be done decently and in order.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
corruption_summary: Commonwealth whose Consensus of Sandomierz in 1570 and Warsaw Confederation of 1573 gave the Reformation wide liberty, which it lost for want of confession, synod and schools.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is a Protestantism that is a party of patrons rather than a church. Poland's Reformed had senators, printing and legal protection, and never completed the ordinary work: no agreed national confession, no discipline a synod could actually enforce on a nobleman, no school system of its own. Titus was left in Crete for exactly this reason, “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5), and in Poland the things that were wanting stayed wanting.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel is handed on by trained and examined men, and that whoever trains the sons will hold the next generation. The charge is to commit the apostolic deposit “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2); in Poland the Jesuits did the committing, in excellent schools, free, and the Protestant nobles sent their boys. The apostolic practice was to appoint officers everywhere a congregation existed, for “when they had ordained them elders in every church” (Act 14:23) is the pattern, and the rule over the whole is that “all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).

“the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — Jesuit schools and Protestant nobles' sons.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the Consensus of Sandomierz, 1570.

pos: n. (the grand duchy whose Reformation gave the Lithuanian language its first printed book in 1547)
etymology: Latin Lituania; Lithuanian Lietuva. The tongue is the most archaic surviving Indo-European language of Europe.
biblical_def: Lithuania is the grand duchy in which the Reformation created a written language. The last pagan state in Europe, baptised only in 1387, it was joined to Poland and ruled by a magnate class whose greatest house, the Radziwills, went Reformed and endowed churches, presses and schools; Mikolajus Radvila the Black paid for the Brest Bible in Polish in 1563. The work that lasted was in Lithuanian. Abraomas Kulvietis founded a school at Vilnius in 1539 and was driven out; Martynas Mazvydas, trained at Konigsberg, published there in 1547 the Catechismusa prasty szadei, the first book ever printed in Lithuanian, a catechism with a rhymed preface and hymns, addressed to a people whose priests mostly could not preach to them; Baltramiejus Vilentas followed with a translation of the Gospels and Epistles, and Jonas Bretkunas translated the whole Bible into Lithuanian by 1590, though it was never printed. Kedainiai became the chief Reformed centre under Radziwill patronage. The Counter-Reformation recovered the magnates and with them the duchy. The dictionary enters Lithuania because its first printed book was a catechism, which is to say that the nation's literature begins with an attempt to teach peasants the faith in words they used.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as instruction by question and answer; a preface as something spoken introductory; pagan as heathen, not Christian; and a grand duchy as the territory of a grand duke.
webster_full: CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
PREFACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.
PAGAN, n. A heathen; a Gentile; one who worships false gods; one not a Christian, Jew or Mahometan.
GRAND DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a grand duke.
RHYME, n. In poetry, a correspondence of sound in the terminating words or syllables of two verses.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Isa 42:6
I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles;

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
corruption_summary: Grand duchy, pagan until 1387, whose Reformation produced the first printed Lithuanian book in 1547 and a complete Lithuanian Bible by 1590.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the baptism of a nation without the teaching of it. Lithuania was declared Christian in 1387 by its grand duke's decision, and a century and a half later its people had no book, no catechism and often no preaching in their language; the old gods were still named in the villages. Mazvydas's preface of 1547 says as much in verse, calling his countrymen to leave what their fathers served and to come and read. The commission is to teach and not merely to baptise: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19) puts the instruction first in the order of the sentence and the work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that conversion is from darkness and must be understood to be real. The apostle's charge was to open men's eyes and “to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18), which cannot be done by a prince's edict. The servant of the Lord is given “for a light of the Gentiles” (Isa 42:6), and the gift at Pentecost answers how: that each man hears “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8), which in 1547 meant a printed Lithuanian catechism.
roots_summary: Greek matheteuo (G3100), to make disciples; Greek skotos (G4655), darkness; Greek dialektos (G1258), the speech of a region.
roots_lines: Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to make a disciple, to teach; “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations”, Matthew 28:19.
Greek baptizo (G907) — to baptize, to wash; “baptizing them in the name of the Father”, Matthew 28:19.
Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness, both natural and moral; “to turn them from darkness to light”, Acts 26:18.
Hebrew or (H216) — light; “for a light of the Gentiles”, Isaiah 42:6.
Greek dialektos (G1258) — the speech of a region; “in our own tongue, wherein we were born”, Acts 2:8.
usage: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19) — a nation baptised by edict in 1387 and untaught.
“in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8) — Mazvydas's Lithuanian catechism, Konigsberg 1547.
“to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18) — the old gods still named in the villages.

pos: n. (the central Polish province about Warsaw whose petty gentry stayed Catholic, and where the Confederation of 1573 was sworn)
etymology: Latin Masovia, Polish Mazowsze, of uncertain Slavic root; the duchy was absorbed into the Polish crown in 1526.
biblical_def: Mazovia is the Polish province that did not go Protestant and thereby decided the commonwealth. Unlike Lesser Poland or Lithuania, where a few great magnates owned enormous estates and could carry whole districts into the Reformed church by their own decision, Mazovia was a land of very numerous and very poor gentry, each with a village or two, proud of their Catholicism and suspicious of the magnates. The Reformation in Poland worked by patronage, and in Mazovia there were no patrons large enough to work with; the province remained solidly Catholic and furnished much of the numerical strength that recovered the kingdom. Its chief town, Warsaw, grew from a provincial seat into the place where the commonwealth's diets met, and it was there in January 1573, at the interregnum after the last Jagiellon died, that the nobility swore the Warsaw Confederation promising to keep the peace between the religions. The Confederation was sworn in the most Catholic province of the kingdom, by men most of whom had no intention of becoming Protestant, which is a fairer account of it than making it a Protestant triumph. The dictionary enters Mazovia because the Reformation's Polish failure was demographic before it was theological.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gentry as people of education and good breeding; an interregnum as the time between two reigns; a diet as an assembly of estates; and patronage as support bestowed on a cause.
webster_full: GENTRY, n. People of education and good breeding; in England, the class of people between the nobility and the yeomanry.
INTERREGNUM, n. The time in which a throne is vacant, between the death or abdication of a king and the accession of his successor.
DIET, n. An assembly of the states or circles of the empire or kingdom; a convention of princes and delegates.
PATRONAGE, n. Special countenance or support; favor or protection bestowed on a person or cause.
PEACE, n. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from war or disturbance.
scriptures: Mat 13:8
But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.
So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
corruption_summary: Central Polish province of numerous poor gentry which stayed Catholic, and whose chief town Warsaw was where the Confederation of 1573 was sworn.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the triumphalist reading of a toleration law, and Mazovia corrects it. The Warsaw Confederation is often presented as the Reformation's Polish victory; it was sworn in the kingdom's most Catholic province by a nobility concerned above all to prevent a French-style civil war during an interregnum, and it bound them to keep the peace rather than to approve each other's doctrine. The dictionary is glad of it on its own terms and declines to misdescribe it. “live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) is a real and apostolic good, and that is what was sworn.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that growth is not in the sower's power, which is the honest conclusion from a province where the preaching reached and the harvest did not come: “neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7). The parable allows for ground that yields and ground that does not, for some seed “fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit” (Mat 13:8) and some did not. Of the men who swore at Warsaw to keep peace between the confessions it may fairly be said, “Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9).

Greek karpos (G2590) — fruit, produce; “fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit”, Matthew 13:8.
Greek eireneuo (G1514) — to be at peace, to live peaceably; “live peaceably with all men”, Romans 12:18.

usage: “but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7) — a province of poor gentry and no Reformed patrons.
“live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18) — the Warsaw Confederation sworn in January 1573.
“Blessed are the peacemakers” (Mat 5:9) — a nobility bent on avoiding a French-style civil war.

pos: n. (the royal Prussian port, Polish Elbląg, Lutheran from 1523, whose gymnasium taught Poles, Germans and Scots together)
etymology: German Elbing, Polish Elbląg, from the Elbing river and the old Prussian settlement of Truso; founded by the Teutonic Order in 1237.
biblical_def: Elbing is one of the three great Hanseatic towns of royal Prussia, with Danzig and Thorn, which took the Reformation by their own civic authority while remaining subjects of a Catholic Polish king. Lutheran preaching began there in 1523 and the council carried the town over in the following years; the king conceded in practice what he could not prevent, and the Prussian towns kept their Lutheran establishment, their guilds and their German law throughout the commonwealth's existence. Elbing's own contribution was educational and mercantile. Its gymnasium, reorganised in 1535 and raised to an academic gymnasium in 1598, taught Latin, Greek, Hebrew and theology to the sons of the Prussian towns and to Poles and Scots; the Eastland Company of English merchants had its staple there from 1579, and a Scottish and English Protestant colony grew up in the town. Elbing and Thorn gave the Lutheran churches of the commonwealth their steadiest ministry, because theirs did not depend on a nobleman. The dictionary enters Elbing because a town council, a school and a trade were enough to keep a church for two centuries where a province of great patrons could not keep one for two generations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gymnasium as a place of exercise or a school; a staple as an established mart of trade; a guild as an incorporated society; and a burgher as an inhabitant of a borough.
webster_full: GYMNASIUM, n. A place where athletic exercises are performed; a school; in Germany, a high school or academy.
STAPLE, n. A settled mart or market; an established town of trade; the principal commodity of a place.
GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some common purpose, as of trade.
BURGHER, n. An inhabitant of a borough or walled town; one who possesses a municipal right.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Act 16:5
And so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
corruption_summary: Royal Prussian port, Lutheran by council decision from 1523, whose academic gymnasium taught Poles, Germans and Scots and whose church outlasted the Polish Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the church that cannot survive a change of patron, which Elbing avoided by being owned by nobody. Its ministers were called and paid by a town council answerable to its own burghers, its school was endowed by the same body, and the Polish crown could remove neither. The result was a congregation that went on quietly for two hundred years doing what the apostle commends, that men “study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11), and the churches so established are described in one line: “so were the churches established in the faith, and increased in number daily” (Act 16:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a church's investment in its own school, which is how doctrine is handed to the next set of officers. The apostolic charge is to commit what has been heard “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and an academic gymnasium teaching Hebrew to merchants' sons is a literal obedience to it. The promise over the whole arrangement is the old one, that if you “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6), when he is old he will not depart from it.

Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, trustworthy; “commit thou to faithful men”, 2 Timothy 2:2.
Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train, to instruct; “Train up a child in the way he should go”, Proverbs 22:6.

usage: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2) — the academic gymnasium of 1598.
“study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — a Hanseatic church owned by its own burghers.
“were the churches established in the faith” (Act 16:5) — two centuries of Lutheran ministry under a Catholic king.

pos: n. (the northernmost port of ducal Prussia, Lithuanian Klaipėda, the frontier post of the Lutheran mission to the Lithuanians)
etymology: German Memel, from the Memel or Nemunas river; Lithuanian Klaipėda, the castle founded by the Teutonic Order in 1252.
biblical_def: Memel is the Baltic port at the top of ducal Prussia where German Lutheranism met the Lithuanian-speaking countryside, and the meeting produced books. The town itself was small, a timber and grain harbour at the mouth of the Curonian lagoon, but its hinterland was Prussian Lithuania, a district settled by Lithuanian-speaking peasants under the duke of Prussia's Lutheran establishment, and the duchy made a deliberate policy of serving them in their own language. Ministers of the Memel and Tilsit districts were expected to preach in Lithuanian; the catechisms, hymnals, Gospel books and finally Jonas Bretkunas's complete Bible translation of 1590 were made for these congregations and not for the grand duchy to the east, which was Catholic. Lithuanian religious literature therefore begins in Prussia, among peasants whose own princes across the border were giving their patronage to the Jesuits. Memel was burned by the Swedes in 1678 and devastated by the plague of 1709, which killed a great part of the Prussian Lithuanians. The dictionary enters Memel because the standing argument for serving a small people in its own tongue was settled on this frontier by men who simply did it, parish by parish, for two centuries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a frontier as the border of a country; a lagoon as a shallow lake near the sea; a hinterland as the country behind a port; and a hymnal as a collection of hymns.
webster_full: FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
LAGOON, n. A shallow lake or channel near or communicating with the sea, often enclosed by a bar.
HARBOR, n. A port or haven for ships; a lodging or place of entertainment; a shelter.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans in honor of some deity; a sacred lyric.
PARISH, n. The precinct or territorial jurisdiction of a secular priest, or the inhabitants belonging to the same church.
scriptures: Act 2:11
Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
corruption_summary: Northernmost port of ducal Prussia whose Lithuanian-speaking hinterland was served in its own language, producing the first Lithuanian catechisms, hymnals and Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the calculation that a people too few to matter may be served in somebody else's language. Prussian Lithuania held perhaps a few tens of thousands of peasants; every argument of economy said to preach to them in German, as Livonia preached to the Estonians, and the duchy decided otherwise and required Lithuanian of its ministers. The vision of the end of things vindicates the decision, for the multitude before the throne is gathered “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9), which is a list that counts no one too few.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour Scripture gives to the men who carry the message to such places. “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” (Rom 10:15) is said of messengers, not of their audience size, and the prophet's original is the same: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7). What those feet brought to the Memel parishes was the thing asked at Pentecost, that men should “hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11).
